properties.title: 1938 aerial photograph (PennPilot)
John Swisshelm buys the grist mill
properties.detail: Valley Forge veteran John Swisshelm buys the mill and builds a log cabin in Nine Mile Run Hollow. The mill likely stood near today's S. Braddock Ave. and W. Swissvale Ave.

properties.title: The Jackson family's log cabin
properties.detail: "The land on which this community center is located was the site of a log cabin built in the year 1837 by George and Elizabeth Jackson... Leaving Philadelphia and crossing the Allegheny Mountains in a covered wagon." (Other sources give 1820 for the cabin.)

properties.title: Jane Grey Swisshelm dies at the old homestead
properties.detail: Editor, abolitionist, Civil War nurse, women's-rights advocate; died 22 Jul 1884 "in old homestead on this site." The neighborhood was renamed for her in 1939.

properties.title: Duck Hollow: mill and railroad workers' houses, post office, general store
properties.detail: Houses built for mill and railroad workers from about the 1880s; the hollow once had its own post office and general store. Nickname "Skeetersville."

properties.title: Swisshelm Park Primitive Methodist Church begins
properties.detail: 241 Homestead St.; "a work that began in 1898," long the neighborhood's only church.

properties.title: Swisshelm School (Colfax No. 4) built
properties.detail: 125 Whipple St.; built 1904 to replace an 1898 four-room frame school; closed 1975.

properties.title: Olmsted proposes a great park in the valley
properties.detail: Frederick Law Olmsted Jr.: "perhaps the most striking opportunity noted for a large park is the valley of Nine Miles Run." Ignored.

properties.title: World War I Honor Roll
properties.detail: "Erected by the residents of the 5th District, 14th Ward." Now on the Engine 19 Fire Station, 159 Homestead St.

properties.title: Duquesne Slag buys the valley; 50 years of dumping
properties.detail: 94 acres bought Sept 1922, just before residential zoning (1923); about 20 million tons of slag dumped until ~1972.

properties.title: Residents petition to add the valley to Frick Park
properties.detail: The first of two decades of Civic Association fights against the slag company (1936, 1942, 1946–47, 1950, 1954, 1958).

properties.title: Homestead High Level Bridge opens
properties.detail: Dedicated 20 Nov 1937; replaced Brown's Bridge (1897); renamed Homestead Grays Bridge (2002).

properties.title: Windermere Drive graded (aerial photo)
properties.detail: The 25 Sep 1938 aerial shows the new Windermere loop as bare earth, with almost no houses.

properties.title: "Swisshelm Park" named; community center dedicated
properties.detail: Dedicated 14 Dec 1939. Contest winner Helen Molyneaux, 12; essay prize to Phyllis Gallina, 13. Donor Robert G. Jackson, "the McCandless Township farmer," said his great-grandfather George Jackson built a cabin here in 1820. Residents rebuilt the 20-year-old cow shed themselves; cost about $12,000 instead of $30,000.
properties.source: Pittsburgh Sun-Telegraph, 15 Dec 1939, p. 32; Pittsburgh Press, 31 Dec 1939, p. 43 (both read in the original)

properties.title: World War II Honor Roll
properties.detail: "Erected as a lasting tribute to the men and women of Swisshelm Park who served... in World War II" (Broberg, Balacko, Burg, and many more). Seven local men were killed.

properties.title: First bus: route 72 "Swisshelm Park"
properties.detail: Started 4 Nov 1946; no streetcar had ever run into the neighborhood. The postwar building boom followed.

properties.title: Residents protest a garbage "sanitary fill"
properties.detail: Letters to the Press: "dumping garbage literally at our back doors," with garbage trucks down Commercial St. Whether it was built is unknown; location approximate.
properties.source: Pittsburgh Press, 26 May 1948 p. 10; 19 Sep 1949 p. 14

properties.title: LeBlanc St.: "10 Sit Tight In Battle On Parkway"
properties.detail: Ten of eleven north-side owners refuse the state's offers (about 80% of replacement cost) and face eviction; the north side of the street is taken for the Parkway.

properties.title: Commercial Street Bridge completed
properties.detail: Built Apr 1948 to Apr 1951 ($1.78M, Dinardo Inc.); tunnel spoil filled the valley 100 ft deep for its approach.

properties.title: Squirrel Hill Tunnel opens
properties.detail: Dedicated 5 Jun 1953; $18M, the costliest state highway project to that date.

properties.title: Slag dumping ends
properties.detail: About 17–20 million cubic yards of slag fill the valley.

properties.title: Lipkind House plaque
properties.detail: Onondago St. A house by Peter Berndtson (1909–1972), who followed Frank Lloyd Wright's organic architecture; PHLF plaque 1989.

properties.title: City buys the slag; Summerset rises
properties.detail: URA purchase (1994–95); two years of grading; Summerset home construction from about 2001.

properties.title: Nine Mile Run restored
properties.detail: Army Corps of Engineers restores 2.2 miles of stream ($7.7M).

properties.title: New McFarren Street Bridge into Duck Hollow
properties.detail: Replaces the one-lane, 8-ton bridge that was Duck Hollow's only road in.

properties.title: Commercial Street Bridge replacement
properties.detail: $95M PennDOT project from Jun 2024; I-376 reopened after a bridge slide in Jul 2026.

properties.title: Last slag parcel capped; solar field planned
properties.detail: About 70 acres lower in the valley: capping from 2024–25, a 15-acre solar field (2027) and a 55-acre Frick Park extension. Location approximate.

properties.name: LeBlanc Street
properties.history: Called Leland St. in the 1910 census, Lippert St. in 1920 and 1930, "Lippert or Le Blanc" in 1940, and Le Blanc by 1950 (the 1939 plat prints "Le Blanc St. (Leland) (Lippert)"). Laid out as Miss S. D. Bryan's subdivision (Plan Book 19, p. 78), inside the city line. Home to many Swedish-born families (1910–1950 censuses). In 1950 the state took the north (odd-numbered) side for the Penn-Lincoln Parkway after ten of eleven owners fought eviction.
properties.source: Hopkins 1939 Pl. 35; U.S. censuses 1910–1950; Pittsburgh Sun-Telegraph, 11 Apr 1950, p. 6

properties.name: Windermere Drive
properties.history: Laid out on Robert G. Jackson's "Ye Olde Swissvale Farme Plan" (Plan Book 35, p. 176), on the old Jackson farm. Not on the 1923 plat; bare graded earth in the 1938 aerial; most houses built in the early 1950s. The community center (1050 Windermere) began as the Jackson barn.

properties.name: Commercial Street
properties.history: Graded through the valley in 1907 (City Photographer, 12 Sep 1907). The old road down to Nine Mile Run now passes under the Parkway's Commercial Street Bridge (1948–51; being replaced 2024–27). In 1948–49 residents feared garbage trucks "funneling" down it to a proposed sanitary fill.

properties.name: Homestead Street
properties.history: Part of the North Homestead Plan (Homestead Bank & Life Insurance Co.). Photographed house by house on 27 Jan 1921. Home of the Primitive Methodist church (241, from 1898) and the fire house (No. 6 Engine House in 1921; Engine 19 today at 159, with the WWI honor roll).

properties.name: Whipple Street
properties.history: Formerly West Street (1939 plat). Site of the Swisshelm School (125 Whipple, 1904–1975), called "Colfax School No. 4" in 1920. Photographed 1907 and 1920.

properties.name: Pocono Street
properties.history: Formerly South and Pitt Street (1939 plat). Its east end was the city line with Swissvale in 1921. New steps at Pocono and Aurora (now Arline) photographed 1923.

properties.name: Onondago Street
properties.history: Formerly Black Oak (1939 plat). Swisshelm Park playground at 1279 Onondago; the Lipkind House (Peter Berndtson) further west.

properties.name: Nevada Street
properties.history: Formerly North Street (1939 plat). The main road along the neighborhood's north side to Swissvale.

properties.name: Blackhawk Street
properties.history: Photographed in Aug 1920 with a group of boys in the street, and at its corner with Commercial in Jan 1921.

properties.name: Love Street
properties.history: "Dutch Row": five frame houses among the first buildings in the neighborhood (photo c. 1911).

properties.name: Blackmore Street
properties.history: Duck Hollow. One house is about 115 years old (c. 1900). Mill and railroad workers' houses, a post office, and a general store once stood in the hollow.

properties.name: McFarren Street
properties.history: Duck Hollow's only road in; its new bridge (2020) replaced a one-lane, 8-ton span. Duck Hollow is in Swisshelm Park but reached only through Squirrel Hill.

properties.name: Old Browns Hill Road
properties.history: The old road down to Brown's Bridge (1897) at the river; the 1927 City Photographer view of Nine Mile Run was taken from here.

properties.name: Summerset Drive
properties.history: Built from about 2001 on top of "Brown's Dump," the slag heap dumped 1922–1972.

properties.name: Nine Mile Run Trail
properties.history: Follows Nine Mile Run, buried under slag for 50 years and restored 2003–2007 by the Army Corps of Engineers. Olmsted called the valley "the most striking opportunity" for a great park (1910).

properties.name: Penn-Lincoln Parkway East
properties.history: I-376. Cut through in 1948–53: the Commercial Street Bridge (1951) and Squirrel Hill Tunnel (1953). Its path took the north side of LeBlanc Street in 1950.

properties.name: Second Avenue (Braddock's Field Plank Road)
properties.history: The old Braddock's Field Plank Road along the Monongahela below Swisshelm Park, shown as Second Avenue ("not open" at its east end) on the 1939 plat. Today no road runs here; the rail line and the riverfront trail occupy the corridor.

properties.name: "Second Ave. Relocation" (planned)
properties.history: A planned relocation of Second Avenue north of the Baltimore & Ohio tracks, drawn on the 1939 plat. Not built as a through road.

properties.name: Arline Street (formerly Aurora)
properties.history: Aurora Street on the 1923 plat, renamed Arline by 1939 and marked "not open." Not in today's street data. The 1923 City Photographer photo of steps "at Pocono and Aurora Streets" was taken near here.

properties.name: McCoy Way
properties.history: The alley behind the north (odd-numbered) side of LeBlanc Street. The houses it served were taken for the Penn-Lincoln Parkway in 1950; the alley is not in today's street data.

properties.name: Brush Way
properties.history: An alley through John J. Lovas's 1923 lot plan between Onondaga and Commercial Streets. By 1939 the land belonged to Robert George Jackson in large lots, and no street was ever built.

properties.name: City line, 1923 (Pittsburgh / Swissvale)
properties.history: The Pittsburgh–Swissvale boundary as drawn on the 1923 Hopkins plat (traced from the pink line). It matches the east edge of today's Swisshelm Park within about 10–25 m, and the 1939 plat shows the same line: the city line here has not moved since at least 1923.

properties.title: Alliance Chapel (1911 plat)
properties.detail: The 1911 Hopkins plat shows an "Alliance Chapel" at Nightingale and Commercial, near Whipple (lot of M. Callender). Probably an early mission church; later history unknown.

properties.title: Footbridge over Commercial St. (1911 plat)
properties.detail: The 1911 plat marks a "Foot Bridge" across Commercial Street between Whipple and Homestead, where the street ran in a cut.

properties.title: Colfax Land Co. and the McKelvey Grove Plan
properties.detail: In 1911 the west side (Olivia, Uptegraff, Love, Pocono, Goodman, Ober, Philander streets) was the McKelvey Grove Plan: hundreds of 25-ft lots, almost all still empty. The Colfax Land Co. owned the triangle between Onondago and Commercial. "Spring St." (later Satire, now Satyr Way) ran between Whipple and Homestead.

properties.title: Residents organize in the cow shed
properties.detail: "Four years ago a group of residents of North Homestead... met in an old barn on the Swissvale Farm and organized a community center." The "20-year-old cow shed" became the Sarah Jackson Black Community Center.

properties.title: Swissvale station on the Pennsylvania Railroad
properties.detail: Built by 1852 to serve four trains a day and named for the Swisshelms' farm; later served the Pitcairn Local. Exact depot site not found (placed near the rail line).
properties.source: Fanzo, Cultural Survey of Swissvale (1992), p. 3

properties.title: Union Switch & Signal ("the Switch")
properties.detail: Westinghouse's railroad-signal works, on the old Allegheny Car shops site: 50+ acres, 4,200+ workers in the early 1970s. Seven-month strike in 1982; closed 1985, demolished 1986; now Edgewood Towne Centre.

properties.title: Frick Park buys the Pittsburgh Country Club (Riverview Hill)
properties.detail: The Frick trustees paid $197,500 for the 84-acre golf course and riding facility along Beechwood Blvd, carrying the park southwest toward Swisshelm Park. Its clay went into the red clay tennis courts on S. Braddock Ave.
properties.source: Frick Park Historic Landmark nomination (2023), pp. 4–5, 8

properties.title: Blue Slide Playground
properties.detail: On Beechwood Blvd at English Lane. Planned 1959; opened between 1960 and 1963 (sources disagree). The slide was originally red.

properties.title: Frick Environmental Center
properties.detail: Opened 1979 (funded by Childs Frick); destroyed by fire in 2002; rebuilt 2016 as a LEED Platinum building.

properties.title: Mon-Fayette Expressway plan threatens the riverfront
properties.detail: The Turnpike's route from Route 51 to I-376 was in design from 2004; the leg toward Oakland was dropped in 2015 and work on the extension halted in 2017. Duck Hollow residents saw it as a threat.
properties.source: PA Turnpike; Tube City Online, Mar 2017; City Paper, Nov 2011

properties.title: Nine Mile Run trail bridge to Duck Hollow
properties.detail: A new trail bridge links Frick Park's Nine Mile Run trail to Duck Hollow (work from late 2009; completion target May 2010).

properties.title: Duck Hollow trailhead and seawall
properties.detail: The seawall at the end of Old Browns Hill Rd was once "a major transfer point between the river and the huge slag piles up Nine Mile Run." Today it's the trailhead for the Three Rivers Heritage Trail (Duck Hollow segment). Date of the trail's opening not found.
properties.source: Uncovering PA; Friends of the Riverfront
